speechtext: The house resumed, from Thursday, March 27, consideration of the motion of Mr. Abbott for committee of supply, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Wright.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: QUESTION AS TO COMBAT PAY FOR SOLDIERS IN KOREA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to support the amendment which was moved by my desk-mate on March 25, as recorded in Hansard at page 771. That amendment, which I had the honour to second, reads as follows:
That all the words after the word "that" to the end of the question be struck out, and the following words be substituted therefor:
"this house regrets that the government has failed to take effective steps to achieve the implementation of article 2 of the North Atlantic treaty."
We in this group, Mr. Speaker, feel that the offering of that amendment is one of the most significant events in the history of the discussion of the North Atlantic treaty which has taken place in this house since the treaty was first presented to this parliament. Despite some of the comments that have been made by certain government supporters during the course of this debate, we feel that the offering of this amendment actually strengthens the support that this country can give to NATO, and is indeed very timely.
As a matter of fact, that point was emphasized in an editorial which appeared in the Ottawa Citizen on Saturday, March 29, and which read in part as follows:
While strenuous efforts are being made to erect the free world's military defences, attempts to strengthen the economies of European countries, as well as of backward areas, do not appear to be

Supply-External Affairs making comparable headway. The lack of confidence motion introduced into the House of Commons by the C.C.F.. on grounds that the government has failed to implement article 2 of the North Atlantic treaty, is therefore timely.
There are other sentences in that Citizen editorial to which I shall refer later in my remarks, but at the moment I introduce that comment as to the timeliness of the amendment which is before the house.
I suggest that those who have objected to foreign policy being the subject of a want of confidence motion are reflecting on the essence and the genius of democracy. Surely it is essential to our democratic way that there should be free discussion of all issues that are important. Nothing is more important to us in this country or anywhere in the world today than the international situation, and it would be a strange situation if every one of us in this house had exactly the same ideas as to all aspects of foreign policy. We differ, and express those differences, on a great many matters that are of much less importance. I suggest, therefore, that if there are differences of opinion about certain aspects of our foreign policy, it is our duty to express those differences on the floor of this house.
I feel that the issue which is presented in this amendment is very clear. Likewise I believe it is the most important issue there is in connection with our country's support of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization. The wording of this amendment, both by what it says and what it omits saying, makes it very clear as to the point at which we are really critical of the present government. The amendment makes it clear, as did the statement issued by the C.C.F. national council a month ago, and as did the first speech on this question in this house by my leader on March 6 and other speeches that have been made since, that the C.C.F. supports in full the principle of NATO. There is no question about that, and the amendment makes it clear.
In the second place, I would point out that there is no question as to our support of the contention that NATO involves military defences which involve commitments in terms of manpower and in terms of huge expenditures. There is nothing in this amendment touching that aspect of the matter, which I suggest is significant. It makes it clear that we are not critical of the underlying assumption in NATO, namely, that there must be military preparation and military defences.
In the third place, this amendment, by virtue of the fact it sticks to one point, makes it clear that we are not unduly critical of the government on the score of mutual aid-


and by "mutual aid" we mean what is referred to in article 3 of the North Atlantic treaty, namely assistance amongst the NATO powers with respect to the supplying of military equipment.
The other day the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson), when my deskmate was speaking, made an interjection with reference to the mutual aid that is being provided for in the estimates that are now before the house. That has to do with the supplying of arms to our partners in NATO, and we welcome the fact that this government is playing some part in the implementation of article 3 of the treaty.
So far so good. In other words, on those three points, this amendment offers no criticism, support of NATO in principle, support of the necessity of military defences and support of what is being done in terms of mutual aid, or in other words the implementation of article 3 of the treaty. What we are critical of, and strongly critical, is clearly set out in the amendment which is before the house. We are critical of the government in that it has fallen down with respect to article 2 of the North Atlantic treaty, and in that it has failed to give a lead in seeking the implementation of that article, calling as it does for economic aid.
Let it be clear that there is a distinction between mutual aid as provided for in article 3 of the treaty and economic aid as provided for in article 2. Mutual aid, as I said a moment ago, involves the provision of arms and military equipment. Economic aid involves contributions of money, food and raw materials in order to enable other members of NATO to develop and strengthen their basic economy and to better the health, security and well-being of their people.
I want to bring to my support evidence of my stand when I say that the government has fallen down with respect to seeking to achieve the implementation of article 2 of the North Atlantic treaty. That is the whole point of this party's criticism; and I believe it is valuable and constructive criticism that we are offering at this stage in this debate on external affairs. A few moments ago I quoted from part of the editorial that appeared in Saturday's Ottawa Citizen. I now quote another sentence or two from that same editorial:
Article 2 calls for economic collaboration, and although Canada had a large part in introducing this into the treaty, Canada has not led the way in its implementation.
Another item of evidence that I would introduce is something I referred to a moment ago. When my deskmate, the hon. member for Melfort (Mr. Wright), was speaking the other

day, at the time he introduced this amendment, the Secretary of State for External Affairs interjected that he felt that my colleague was going a little too far in his statement that we were not providing any economic aid. What was the interjection made by the Secretary of State for External Affairs? He asked what my colleague thought of the $300 million in this year's estimates for mutual aid. That is exactly the point, Mr. Speaker. When we press the government as to what they are doing in terms of economic aid they say:	Look at what we are
doing in terms of mutual aid. We do not deny that this government is doing something with respect to mutual aid; but the inability of the minister to refer to anything other than mutual aid indicates our point, namely, that article 2 which calls for non-military economic aid is not being implemented by this government.
Similarly, Mr. Speaker, when the parliamentary assistant to the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Lesage) got into this debate with respect to the whole question of the economic aspects of our foreign policy, he dealt only with what is being done under the Colombo plan and under the technical assistance program. In both of those cases he was forced to point out that Canada has not yet spent the full amount of the sums of money that were appropriated for even that kind of economic aid. He of course said nothing at all about economic aid under the provisions of the North Atlantic treaty, for the reason that there is none. In other words, Mr. Speaker, there really is no argument as to the fact of the situation. We are pulling our weight, some of us may feel, so far as the military aspect is concerned. We are glad that something is being done in terms of mutual aid with respect to arms. But the plain fact of the matter is that nothing is being done by this government with respect to economic aid, to assist the economies-the standard of living, the productive capacity-of the countries that are associated with us in this North Atlantic coalition, let alone backward countries in other parts of the world, apart from the bit of help that is being given under the Colombo plan and under the United Nations technical assistance program.
One other bit of evidence that I should like to give in support of the proposition that we are doing nothing in terms of economic aid again involves quoting from the Secretary of State for External Affairs. He has long since learned that we are fond of quoting him against himself, and I do so again. When he was speaking in this debate -indeed it was the speech that opened this present debate on external affairs-on Friday, March 21, 1952, as reported at page 666 of 55704-64J
Supply-External Affairs Hansard, he said something that I should like to quote. At that point he was dealing with another phase of NATO affairs. He was dealing, in fact, with the armament and financial goals set at Lisbon, and he was trying to deal with a point that had been raised by my leader, the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell). This is what the minister said:
At the same time we should not, I think, exaggerate the importance of what, after all, are only decisions which are yet to be converted into action. The prestige of NATO must not be based upon illusions. One easy and tempting illusion these days is that a resolution at an international conference is always the same as the result. A resolution is a decision to act; but it is action which produces results.
In other words, when he was looking at the military side of the picture the Secretary of State for External Affairs said: Do not pay any attention to that NATO release; do not pay any attention to the figures that have been bandied about in the press. Look at the results. That is what counts. But when, in that same speech, he got over to the question of economic aid, what did he do? He gave us the very same sort of thing which he had said, in respect of military preparations, was without value. He gave us the report of resolutions; he gave us words, and the clear admission that literally nothing was being done. As reported at page 672 of Hansard for March 21, the minister will recall that he was interrupted first by my deskmate, the hon. member for Melfort (Mr. Wright), and later by myself. Back at page 671, as he is there reported, the minister had been assuring us that the economic aspects of NATO had not been overlooked, and he gave us a few broad statements as to what was being thought about. He gave us these words, these resolutions which, he told the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar, in respect of military preparations, were not to be exaggerated. As a result of the nebulous nature of these statements, my colleague naturally felt disposed to ask the obvious question, and this was it:

maintopic: QUESTION AS TO COMBAT PAY FOR SOLDIERS IN KOREA
speechtext:
Can the minister say, in concrete
terms, what has been done to date?
Here was the answer:

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: QUESTION AS TO COMBAT PAY FOR SOLDIERS IN KOREA
speechtext:
I cannot give any information in
concrete terms as to what has been done in the field to which I have just referred. Indeed, very little has been done in the field of non-military co-operation.
Yet, Mr. Speaker, that is the whole sum and substance of article 2 of the treaty which this government, prodded by us, played a part in getting written into the treaty. The minister now admits that very little is being done about it.
A little further down on the same page we And it was pointed out to the minister that surely whatever is being talked about in this

Supply-External Affairs field should not be regarded as a military secret; yet the minister asserted that because no final decisions had been taken, anything contained in the report laid before the NATO council on other than military decisions could not be disclosed at this time. So what we have is a few words, some high-sounding resolutions, and anything that is involved in those high-sounding resolutions is locked away in secrecy.
Further down on the same page, page 672 of Hansard, it will be found I asked the minister this question:

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: QUESTION AS TO COMBAT PAY FOR SOLDIERS IN KOREA
speechtext:
Can he say whether there was any discussion of any budgetary arrangements for carrying out any of these economic proposals?
This is the reply:

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: QUESTION AS TO COMBAT PAY FOR SOLDIERS IN KOREA
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, there was a discussion of budgetary arrangements for NATO generally and there was an estimate made by the experts who worked with us on this committee as to how much these proposals would cost. They will cost a considerable amount. They include such items as exchanges of students and that kind of thing. But I am not in a position to give exact figures in that regard at the present time. They will not cost much in relation. I might add, to our total defence program.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: QUESTION AS TO COMBAT PAY FOR SOLDIERS IN KOREA
speechtext:
You are saying that before we do.
All these quotations that I have given, Mr. Speaker, make it crystal clear that the minister himself, as well as others, newspaper editors, commentators, and students of foreign affairs generally, recognize that Canada is doing nothing in terms of economic aid under the provisions of NATO, and it would appear similarly that Canada has done little if anything to try to persuade NATO itself to move in the direction of implementing article 2 of the treaty. In fact, I believe Canada has actually turned down a specific request from NATO for economic aid.
We feel, as I said a moment ago, that in offering these criticisms we are playing a constructive part with respect to Canadian foreign policy at this stage of affairs; indeed we believe it is a constructive part in the affairs of the world itself; for we are convinced, as are a great many others, that the peace of the world, the possibility of our North Atlantic coalition holding together, indeed, the possibility of the whole world holding together, depends upon the extent to which we can move in the direction of economic aid on a mutual basis so that the economies and the well-being of our various countries might be strengthened.
That has to be done, as I see it, with two objectives in view. On the one hand, it has to be done because not until we establish, or help to establish, healthy economies, healthy

societies in all the nations of the world, particularly the backward ones-not until we do that are we going to stem the tide of communist advance.
After all, communism makes its headway not so much by force of arms as it does by the spread of ideas, and those ideas spread far too easily in areas where there is poverty, disease or economic ill-health. The minister knows just as well as we do-and he has said it often, said it in better words than I can command-that we have to work on that aspect of the problem if we are going to stem communist advances.
But not only is it necessary to provide economic aid to help other countries to keep on their feet for that reason; it is also necessary as a phase of our military preparations. Indeed, Mr. Speaker, that is well set out in a number of quotations that I have before me, some of which I should like to refer to. A few days ago my colleague, the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Stewart), referred to the Christian Science Monitor of Monday, March 24, 1952, the main article of which is headed: "Gruenther says economic aid is as vital as arms." The story is one from Washington quoting General Alfred M. Gruenther speaking before the senate foreign relations committee on behalf of his chief, General Dwight D. Eisenhower, and saying on behalf of General Eisenhower what is set out under the heading, namely, that economic aid is as vital as arms.
A few days later, on March 26, 1952, the Christian Science Monitor dealt with this question again in a special article entitled "The American scene", written by Roscoe Drummond, chief of the Washington news bureau of the Christian Science Monitor. I find this a very interesting and objective account of the position taken by General Gruenther before the senate foreign relations committee. He says, if I may take the opportunity of paraphrasing it in part, that General Gruenther was particularly strong in his plea both for mutual aid and for economic aid, and at one point-I read this because, as I say, it answers some of the arguments put up by the other side-Roscoe Drummond says this:
It needs to be remembered that Europe is just getting back on its feet economically after the havoc of the war. Continued economic aid. as in the Marshall plan, would be unjustified if it were not for the speed and scope of the defence build-up since Korea.
From my point of view, if I may interject here, I am not sure that the continued economic aid by the Marshall plan would not be a good idea, even if defence preparations had not been speeded up. I am one of those who feel that the way to guarantee the future

peace of the world is to think of the world as one world and try to improve the economies and the standards of living of all peoples the world round. There are others who take a different view, but even those who take the other view should pay attention to what is said in the article I am now quoting from the Christian Science Monitor. This particular paragraph goes on to say:
But increased expenditures for defence means that Europe must spend more dollars to obtain the needed raw materials and machinery for production, food for factory workers, plus fuels, coal, and oil. It also means that because defence spending diverts manpower, materials, and industrial capacity away from production for export, Europe is able to earn fewer dollars. This is why western Europe needs some economic aid for defence support.
That, I may say again, is Roscoe Drummond's summary of the testimony of General Gruenther before the senate foreign relations committee when he appeared there on behalf of his chief, General Eisenhower. In other words, Mr. Speaker, even those whose main interest is in the defence aspect rather than in building up economies, for the sake of the standard of living of the people, even those whose main interest is in military preparations, admit it is necessary to have economic aid so that the economies of these countries would be well based and able to produce sufficient military defences.
The Ottawa Citizen said the same thing in its editorial to which I have already referred. I quote again from that editorial:
Yet if the military superstructure is to be built on a solid social and economic foundation, in which the peoples of the free world can find confidence in their existing institutions and hope for the future, this fact must be faced. Otherwise, for lack of sufficient sacrifices made now by the wealthier nations,-
That includes the United States and Canada.
-the first strong wind from Siberia is as likely as not to blow the military superstructure down, just as the large French armies were scattered in 1940 before their lesser German opponents.
Another quotation which I should like to draw to the attention of the house appeared in the New York Times of Tuesday, December 4, 1951. It was a special dispatch to the New York Times from Washington, dated December 3, reporting an address of Mr. Richard M. Bissell, Junior, deputy director of the mutual security agency. This dispatch puts within quotation marks these words, spoken by Mr. Bissell:
It has become a major heresy in Washington to suggest that continued economic progress was intended as part of the rearmament program.
Hon. members will please note this:
Actually nothing is more necessary than economic and social health of the participating countries if
Supply-External Affairs the rearmament program is to be achieved. A well-knit social fabric is necessary to the support of any military effort.
That is the end of the paragraph within quotation marks, but further on in the same article I read:
European rearmament will fail, no matter how much money the United States put into the effort, unless drastic changes are made in the structure, as well as the productivity, of the western European economy. Mr. Bissell told his luncheon audience.
And so, Mr. Speaker, you have it on every hand. The Secretary of State for External Affairs agrees with us-in fact, it is his own idea-that to stem the tide of communism we have got to improve the economies of those other countries, we have got to improve the standard of living, the well-being of these people. If we are going to do that we may have to make some sacrifices in terms of economic aid.
Those who think particularly and technically about the military side feel likewise that economic aid to the economies of those countries is necessary, and yet, despite all that, article 2 still remains an article in the treaty which Canada helped to get there, but about which thus far she seems to have done very little, if anything at all. I quote also a sentence or two from the Economist under date of March 1, 1952. As a matter of fact the article was entitled "Security second". I would ask hon. members to note this:
A bankrupt Britain, a Britain unable to buy raw materials or to preserve sterling as an international currency, cannot be safe or contribute to the safety of others. When the need is so pressing, economic solvency must rank before military security.
I find that something of that view was expressed the other day by the hon, member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker). If I do him an injustice in putting it that way, then he is here to correct me. The hon. member, speaking before the Empire club at the Royal York hotel in Toronto last Thursday, dealt with the bulwark Great Britain is in the free world, and urged substantial contributions by Canada to Great Britain. The heading in the Globe and Mail for Friday, March 28, reads "Diefenbaker urges $200 million in cash and food for Britain." This is a report of the speech he made last Thursday in Toronto. There we have another authority-and I hope he will not mind my using the term in reference to him-suggesting that economic aid is vital at this juncture in world history.
The hon. member for Lake Centre put it down, in concrete terms, that not only is economic aid necessary, but Canada should do something about it, that Canada had had

Supply-External Affairs something to do with getting article 2 into the treaty, and should come along with $100 million or $200 million by way of aid to Britain, partly in cash and partly in food.
I should like to point out that on the same day the hon. member was making that speech in Toronto, the same idea was being put forth in the House of Commons by my colleague the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Stewart), speaking in support of the amendment moved by the hon. member for Melfort (Mr. Wright). He suggested precisely the same figure of $100 million or $200 million by way of economic aid to NATO countries. Let me be fair and say that there is a slight difference. The hon. member for Lake Centre was asking that the whole of the contribution go to Great Britain or perhaps the commonwealth countries, while the hon. member for Winnipeg North was proposing that that should be the possible measure of our economic aid to NATO countries. At any rate they were both suggesting the same thing, and I think both of them were using sound judgment; both were making a suggestion that could play an important part in furthering the peace of mankind.
The same day the hon. member for Lake Centre was making that suggestion in Toronto, his leader in the House of Commons, speaking shortly after the hon, member for Winnipeg North, had used precisely the same figures as those used in Toronto by the hon. member for Lake Centre-as I say, speaking shortly after my colleague from Winnipeg North, the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) said that he would vote against the amendment moved by the hon. member for Melfort, even though it asked for the very same thing, namely, economic aid to NATO countries.

Mr. Speaker, with regard to the latter comments of the leader of the opposition, I would point out that both speeches were made on the same day in different places, and it is unlikely that either of the hon. members knew what the other was saying on that day. And then he went on to say:

And then I interjected to point out that it had been moved by the hon. member for Melfort, and seconded by myself. Might I remind the hon. member that he had the unique distinction of having this party and other parties in the house support him in another motion within a day or so of this very statement.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: QUESTION AS TO COMBAT PAY FOR SOLDIERS IN KOREA

maintopic: QUESTION AS TO COMBAT PAY FOR SOLDIERS IN KOREA

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: QUESTION AS TO COMBAT PAY FOR SOLDIERS IN KOREA
speechtext:
That reminds me of a story I once heard of a woman who said that they just put ideas into her head. However, I was referring to various quotations and authorities for my contention that nothing
Supply-External Affairs is more important at this time than the implementation of article 2 of the North Atlantic treaty and economic aid generally, not only to NATO nations but to backward countries in other parts of the world. I think hon. members would do well to read a few excerpts from "Mr. President", an article which appears in this month's Reader's Digest and which contains some intimate ideas of President Truman. For example, on pages 239 and 240 I find the following quotation direct from Mr. Truman:
I consider point four a practical answer to a growing crisis in a world torn between aggression and peace. We have bought time at great expense and a terrible cost of lives and fortune, and now we must use that time intelligently and courageously. We face serious trouble unless we realize that our own welfare and that of the rest of the world depend upon the constant and dynamic expansion of the world's resources. Fear that the world is growing too small is groundless. There is room, shelter and food for millions more if we put our know-how to work.
President Truman went on to deal with the situation in certain specific areas of the world and pointed out in precise terms what could be done in the way of assistance from North America to help develop the economies and productivity of other parts of the world in such a way as to guarantee the future peace and happiness of mankind.
Because of the extreme importance, as I have tried to lay it before the house, of economic aid, I suggest that the terms of our amendment cannot be evaded by calling it a want of confidence motion, saying that it is not a good idea to introduce such a motion with respect to foreign policy, or squirming around it in any way. The plain fact of the matter is that in presenting this motion at this time we do so because we believe it will strengthen the hands of the Secretary of State for External Affairs, both in the government of this country and in the councils of NATO. I have no doubt that he needs strength for his ideas in both of those places.
While I am on my feet I want to say a few words with respect to a couple of other propositions that I should like to lay before the house at this time. When the Secretary of State for External Affairs was speaking a few days ago he sought to answer my demands of an earlier date for more precise information with respect to the military and financial aspects of the NATO goals and he suggested that Canada was being told her part both in terms of manpower and in terms of dollars, but that we could not expect to have the details for all other countries or indeed the total picture.
I submit that if each of the countries in NATO is allowed to have information with respect to itself, surely we are not children and it should be possible for us to be given

Supply-External Affairs the totals. I urge that that should be done. I press that point for two reasons which I shall try to state quickly. The first is that we need that information in order to be able to decide whether our contribution is as large as it should be, is too large or not large enough. I suggest also that the people of free countries give their best support when they really know what is going on.
The other comment I make, and this is my last, is that I feel that at this juncture of world affairs NATO owes it to itself and to the world to make a clear statement as to our aims in that organization. I consider this somewhat parallel to the situation that existed during world war II when our war aims needed to be stated. I say now that our defence aims need to be stated. I feel that we should make it clear that we are not trying to set in motion a rearmament race that will go on forever, but rather that we are trying-I am speaking now of the military side of the program-to achieve goals of strength which are not ends in themselves but from which we propose to negotiate for the peace of the world.
The phrase "negotiate from strength" is bandied about a great deal. But when and where is the point at which we will be satisfied that we have the strength and that it is time to negotiate? My fear is that this military program can become a snowball which will grow until we have just another rearmament race such as has bedevilled the world all through modern history. Our aim should not be to have a permanent cold war with the danger that it will become a hot war. As I have said already, our aim should be to establish strength from which we can negotiate. But strength is not the end; surely it is a means. It is peace we really want.
On March 18 I said that in my view the greatest burden in the history of the world had been laid upon the NATO countries. We cannot get away from the fact that we are called upon to build up our military preparations and defences. However, every time in history that that has happened it has become a rearmament race which has broken out in war. This time we say that we do not want it to be that. We assert that we do not intend it to go that way this time. If we are going to give meaning to that intention I say we have to make a clear statement of our defence aims as well as the other aims to which I have referred.
I believe that we can prevent the holocaust of a third world war and NATO can play a part in that effort if we do at least the things I have been suggesting this afternoon. I shall repeat them in reverse. First, that we should examine our defence aims and state them

clearly. Second, that so far as the military side of the program is concerned we should have all the information out in the open. Finally, we should concentrate to a much greater extent than has been the case thus far on economic aid which is so important to the peace and well-being of mankind.

Mr. Speaker, with at least one of the observations made by the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat, I agree, and that is when he said that I needed strength. I am going to need that strength, and possibly the house will need some strength also because I will take up a good deal of the time of the house this afternoon in trying to deal with as many of the questions that have been raised during the course of this debate as I have time for and also to deal if I may with the motion which is before the house and which has been explained once more by the hon. member who has just taken his seat.
In dealing with some of the questions that have been raised during the course of this debate and about which information has been requested from the government and about which observations have been made concerning government policy, I should like to begin with Far Eastern affairs. This has taken up a good deal of the time of the discussion. The hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green) complained the other day during his interesting contribution to the debate about the light-hearted way in which I dealt with these questions and that all I had done, to use his words, was to challenge the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Graydon) to a schoolboy debate concerning them.

maintopic: QUESTION AS TO COMBAT PAY FOR SOLDIERS IN KOREA
speechtext: That was on Formosa.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: QUESTION AS TO COMBAT PAY FOR SOLDIERS IN KOREA
speechtext:
On Formosa. The hon. member for Peel complained that I was trying to lead him into an academic discussion on this matter. There could hardly be anything less academic in the world than the situation in the Far East, particularly in Korea and Formosa. Indeed there is so little of the academic about this subject that when the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) began to talk about Far Eastern matters he admitted it was risky to discuss them; and so it is. It is also delicate, and not easy.
A good many references have been made to Formosa. In that connection I asked-and I did not do so in any provocative sense but in the same way that that information had been asked of me-as to the policy of the opposition parties in respect of Formosa and Far Eastern questions. I said I was not sure in my own mind, for instance, what was the

policy of the Progressive Conservative party in respect of that island. They had stated through their spokesmen that they would not permit Formosa to fall into communist hands, and when I heard that statement-which was made more than once-I wondered what was meant by it. Did that mean we should use force to prevent Formosa falling into communist hands? Is it suggested that the United Nations should use force for this purpose, which of course is manifestly impossible? Or is it suggested that Canada and the United States might use force for this purpose? I did not go as far as that. It was suggested that my fault in talking about this matter was that I left the question of Formosa open; and I submit that that is exactly what should be done with it at this time.
At the moment we in the United Nations are pledged at least to try to make peace with communist China over Korea; and negotiations for the first stage of making peace, the armistice stage, are now under way. That is what we are trying to do. Then if we are successful in the first stage we are pledged to discuss other Far Eastern questions. We have taken that pledge in the United Nations. Should we now say that we will never allow Formosa to go back to Peking, if they do not throw out their present government in China? Should we say that, especially when we have subscribed to international agreements recognizing Formosa as part of China, and when we recognize that now sovereignty legally resides in China? I suggest that that would be rigid, dead-end diplomacy, and not very wise diplomacy to follow at this time in this matter. Suppose we had followed the same tactics three or four years ago in respect of Yugoslavia. We would look a little ridiculous now. In discussing this matter the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Graydon) said, at page 675 of Hansard for March 21:
... as I see it today, neither this nor any other government can do more than simply to formulate its Far Eastern policy with respect to Formosa and to red China, on a day-to-day basis.
Personally I think that may be going a little too far in the pursuit of freedom of action; but if it means anything at all-and I suggest it does mean something-it is certainly not what the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green) advocates. It must surely mean that it would be unwise now to say we will not permit Formosa ever to be returned to China if a communist government is in power at Peking.

maintopic: QUESTION AS TO COMBAT PAY FOR SOLDIERS IN KOREA
speechtext: It is not what you said, either.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: QUESTION AS TO COMBAT PAY FOR SOLDIERS IN KOREA
speechtext:
It also means it would be unwise to say now that we will hand it
Supply-External Affairs over to such a government in Peking, or that we would force the people of Formosa to join China under that government. No one on this side of the house has ever suggested that, nor can any reasonable inference be drawn from any statement I have made which would indicate that to be the policy of the government. Ultimately, of course, Formosa must be a question of international discussion and decision, preferably through the United Nations as the Secretary of State for the United States has already intimated.
In such a discussion, which I suppose must come ultimately, there are certain factors which should be taken into consideration by those responsible. The first-and possibly the most important factor of all, though it is very often overlooked-in our discussion of this matter is that the views of the Formosan people themselves should be taken into consideration. They are a people who have not known national freedom, who are in many ways quite separate from the Japanese and Chinese who have ruled over them. Second, consideration must be given to international engagements already undertaken including, I may add, the United Nations charter. Third, consideration should be given to the character and policies of the government or governments of China which may be in power at that time. Fourth, of course, we cannot overlook the fact I have just mentioned, that legally Formosa is part of China. Both Chinese governments insist on that. It is about the only matter on which they are united. The dispute is over which government shall control Formosa.
The leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) seemed even more suspicious than the hon. member for Peel about government policy in regard to Formosa. He got quite rhetorical over the necessity for open diplomacy in this matter. As he said, there must be no secret agreements with regard to Formosa or any other country in the world; there must be no sordid trades dealing with human lives. And he felt that to hand over Formosa to the Peking government of China would be the same brand of appeasement that was represented by what he called the terrible decision at Munich.
Mr. Speaker, in regard to this suggestion I need only say that there is no deal about which we know anything, secret or otherwise, in regard to Formosa; and the bogey of secret diplomacy in this matter is strictly fictitious. The United Nations must decide, and there is not much secret diplomacy these days about the United Nations. Possibly we might make more progress if we had a little more confidential discussion there. Open covenants, yes; but occasionally open covenants confidentially negotiated, after the

Supply-External Affairs principles and purposes of the negotiations have been made known to our own people. I am not sure that would not be more effective and far better for peace and good understanding than the headline and housetop diplomacy on which the Russian communists, who are now the staunchest believers in open diplomacy, insist.
The leader of the opposition also finds something suspicious and secret in alleged arrangements regarding retaliatory action in Korea. In this connection the other evening he enunciated a really strange diplomatic doctrine. I would like to quote from what he said on this point, at page 869 of Hansard for March 27:
The members of this house will recall the assurance which was given that the government of Canada and the government of the United Kingdom were dealing with these problems on the basis of complete confidence and complete understanding.
The problem was what should happen in Korea if there should be renewed aggression there or a renewed offensive in the present aggression. Then he went on:
There was, in fact, more than the suggestion that it was extremely fortunate that the government of the United Kingdom, with our knowledge, had restrained the United States from commitments which might have carried hostilities beyond the mainland of Korea. That being so, there is an explanation due to this house. Was the Canadian government aware of the arrangement between Mr. Attlee and Mr. Morrison on the one hand, and the government of the United States on the other, and of the possible extension of hostilities to the bases on the China coast in the event of pressure which would justify that action under the arrangement which was arrived at?
Further he said:
Either the Canadian government knew of that arrangement or it did not, If it knew of that arrangement, then we in the house should have known of that arrangement in complete detail. If it did not know of that arrangement, then there was not, between the government of the United Kingdom and the government of Canada, that measure of confidence which we had a right to expect. Whichever it was, the disclosure of that fact should persuade every member of this house that if there is one thing above all others which we will insist upon, as members of the Canadian House of Commons, it is that we know every essential fact upon which the future action of this country might be based.
That is the statement made by the hon. member the other night. In other words, what he was saying in the words I have just quoted was that if one government has told us in confidence of an arrangement which it was discussing with another government, we should at once inform this House of Commons about the arrangement in complete detail. That would be a most unusual and unfortunate way in which to conduct diplomacy. It would be a very quick way to alienate your friends and lose your influence with other governments. How could we expect to have friendly governments deal with us


in, and I quote the hon. member's words again, complete confidence and complete understanding, if we told this parliament or the people of Canada at once all that these other governments had told us in confidence?
The fact is, Mr. Speaker, that we knew of these discussions between Washington and London. The fact is also that if they were to be made public that should be done by the governments concerned and not by us. A further fact is that our own policy on this matter-and that is where our responsibility to this parliament lies, not in what is discussed between London and Washington- has already been made clear to this house on more than one occasion. There are no under-the-table deals going on. I do not think I need to delay the house by reading what I said on this very matter in this house both on April 26 and May 7, 1951. Part of the latter speech I repeated in the house last October in respect of our policy in Korea if there were developments there which might, because of Chinese actions, necessitate an extension of the war. I think our policy in that regard has been made quite clear. I do not think there is any room for any misunderstanding as to what it would be.
When the United Kingdom-United States talks were going on in Washington last September, we did at that time restate our views in a message to the state department and to London, so that there would be no misunderstanding there as to where we stood, to the effect that any military action by the unified command which would take effect outside of Korea, should only be taken after consultation between those countries having forces in Korea, unless the safety of the troops made immediate retaliatory action essential and time or circumstances did not permit such consultation.

speechtext: What date was that?

speechtext:
September, 1951. It has also been recognized by us, and by others, that if the armistice talks now going on should break down, and if this should be followed by mass attacks or new aggressions or if the armistice should be signed and afterwards a second aggression committed-I have said this before, too-a new and dangerous situation might arise. Chinese action might make it difficult to restrict the conflict to Korea, no matter how hard we might try to do that. The countries more immediately concerned, because of the fact that they have forces in Korea, have already been discussing amongst themselves what kind of declaration might be made in those circumstances, and what action if any should be considered. But in those discussions I can assure the house that no new commitments have been incurred by Canada.

Along with others we have emphasized the desirability of using United Nations procedures for any formal consultations required or any decisions which may have to be taken.
We have also been discussing with other friendly governments what would be the best procedure for attempting to negotiate a political settlement, once an armistice has been satisfactorily concluded in Korea. Here again in these discussions we have emphasized the importance of the role of the United Nations.
I come now to a question which was raised by the member for Peace River (Mr. Low) and also by the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch), in regard to our ultimate aims in Korea. The hon. member for Peace River wondered if we had backed down from our original purpose, namely, to establish a free, unified, independent and democratic government in Korea. I would reply to that in the following way: As soon as it became seized of the problem in Korea, as far back indeed as 1947, the general assembly of the United Nations has had as its policy the creation of a unified, democratic and independent Korea. It should be emphasized that that is the political purpose to be achieved by peaceful means in accordance with the letter and spirit of the charter of the United Nations. We were trying to do that when the Korean war broke out in June, 1950, thereby adding a new element to the situation. North Korea committed an act of aggression against the Republic of Korea and the United Nations decided, quite properly, that that aggression had to be repelled. A series of resolutions were passed to give effect to that decision. The United Nations now, therefore, is really dealing with two questions-the basic or long term question of the unification and independence of Korea, and the short term question of repelling the aggression committed against the Republic of Korea.
In September and October, 1950, there seemed to be a possibility that the two purposes could be dealt with at once. It seemed likely then that a by-product of the military action taken to repel aggression might be the unification of Korea. If such a possibility existed, the majority of the United Nations wished to take advantage of it, and took action to that end. But as it turned out, that possibility could not be realized at that time because the central people's government of China intervened and the United Nations forces were driven back from North Korea. The United Nations, however, has not abandoned any purpose in Korea. We still hope to repel aggression and prove that it does not profit the aggressor. It is for that purpose we are using force. But while we should be happy to see unification of Korea
Supply-External Affairs result from this use of force for the repulsion of aggression, the United Nations has not been pledged to use force for the sole purpose of bringing about unification. No doubt the unification of Korea will be one of the topics discussed in the political conference which, under the terms of the present draft agreement for an armistice, is to be held within three months after the conclusion of hostilities, if we ever reach that point.
Another Far Eastern subject that arose in the course of the discussions, and indeed was dealt with by several speakers, was this hardy perennial, the Pacific pact. The leader of the opposition inferred from something I said in New York, and repeated in this house, that I have declared in favour of a Pacific pact. I tried to explain that that was not the situation, Mr. Speaker, when I took part in this discussion some days ago, but apparently he was not impressed by my denial or by my explanation. My statement at that time with regard to collective action being necessary in the Pacific does not mean a Pacific pact any more than the statement of Mr. Eden meant a Pacific pact when he said, and I quote from a speech he made in New York:
. . . intervention by force by Chinese communists in southeast Asia . . . would create a situation no less menacing than that which the United Nations met and faced in Korea. In any such event the United Nations should be equally solid to resist it.
But the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green) still insists that we should take the lead here and that pending a broader arrangement we should at least join the trilateral security treaty embracing the United States, Australia and New Zealand. All I can say is that our attitude in this matter is the same as that which I tried to explain to the house last autumn. Our position with regard to a Pacific pact is the same. Within the last few months we have discussed with the governments most concerned whether it is now desirable or possible to broaden this more limited security arrangement into a Pacific pact; and the objections to that broadening remain strong. Those objections are, I think I can say, accepted now as overriding by practically all the countries concerned with Pacific security.

maintopic: QUESTION AS TO COMBAT PAY FOR SOLDIERS IN KOREA
speechtext: Will you not have to come to it eventually?

maintopic: QUESTION AS TO COMBAT PAY FOR SOLDIERS IN KOREA

There is the question of membership at the present time, and I have mentioned that before. There is the question of community of interest. There is the question of the position of metropolitan powers such as France, the United Kingdom and The Netherlands, and their territories in the Pacific. I therefore suggest that while the

Supply-External Affairs advantages of a general Pacific pact are prospective, the difficulties are immediate. Indeed Mr. John Foster Dulles pointed out those difficulties on Friday to the senate committee in Washington. Nevertheless, the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Graydon), as reported at page 676 of Hansard, said:
We must not take the chance of having another Korea. This party has previously called for the consideration of a Pacific pact. It believes that as time moves on the argument in its favour becomes more convincing than ever. The implementation of such a policy would give a measure of stability in the Far East and would enable us to proceed with our plans for the rehabilitation of those areas in the Asiatic free world which are so essential to peace itself.
Our point of view is that the effort to bring that about at this time would produce not stability but instability. Although the time may come when it will be just as desirable to have that kind of pact in the Pacific as it is now desirable to have it in the Atlantic, that time has not yet arrived. As I have said previously-and I should like to repeat it-we are, of course, just as interested in security in the Pacific as we are in security in the Atlantic; and I think our actions indicate that.
There remains the question of the amendment which is before the house, and about which I feel that I should say something on behalf of the government. I must say that I was surprised when this amendment was introduced. It reads as follows:
That all the words after the word "that" to the end of the question be struck out. and the following words be substituted therefor:
"this house regrets that the government has failed to take effective steps to achieve the implementation of article 2 of the North Atlantic treaty."
I was surprised because it was not many months ago-indeed, it was on October 23, 1951-when this house passed, without a dissenting vote, a motion, part of which reads as follows, and I am leaving out the part of it which does not refer to the North Atlantic treaty:
"this house approves of the continuance of Canada's participation in the efforts being made . . . by the North Atlantic treaty nations to deter aggression and promote stability and well-being in the North Atlantic area.
The members of the party who have moved the present resolution found no difficulty in accepting that resolution last October. What has happened between last October and now to change their minds? The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), in his speech a few moments ago, indicated that this kind of resolution would strengthen the hands of those who were supporting the North Atlantic Treaty Organization. I beg leave, Mr. Speaker, to take another view of the effect of this resolution, if it were passed

by this house. It states-and the hon. member for Melfort did not attempt to deny this fact when he introduced it-the refusal of that party to accept the present policy of the government with respect to the North Atlantic Treaty Organization.

I want to say, and as decidedly as I can, that this is not the case. While we do agree with the overall objective, we certainly disagree with the methods by which this government is presently trying to implement that objective.
Why do they disagree? Not, I think, as one might have expected, because the military goals set at Lisbon, although lower than the previous goals, were too high.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: QUESTION AS TO COMBAT PAY FOR SOLDIERS IN KOREA
speechtext:
Not because the North Atlantic Treaty Organization has fallen completely under military control or under American influences, but surprisingly because we have not taken effective steps to implement article 2. Article 2 has been read before, but sometimes its meaning is overlooked, in spite of the number of times it has been read. It reads:
The parties will contribute towards the further development of peaceful and friendly international relations by strengthening their free institutions-
Are we trying to do that?
-by bringing about a better understanding of the principles upon which these institutions are founded,-
Are we trying to do that?
-and by promoting conditions of stability and well-being.
Are we trying to do that? Then the article goes on as follows:
They will seek to eliminate conflict in their international economic policies and will encourage economic collaboration between any or all of them.
Are we trying to do that? I suggest that we are trying to do all of those things which are mentioned in article 2; and nothing else is mentioned in article 2.

In the course of his speech introducing this motion the hon. member for Melfort, who charged me with making at least one irresponsible statement, himself made a few statements which I thought were somewhat irresponsible. He accepts our military expenditures but he complains that we will not give away our materials free and, surprisingly, that we will not accept goods that can be sold in our markets to pay for these materials. He also says that we demand cash on the barrelhead for the necessary materials which these other countries, these friends of ours in NATO, need in order to carry out an effective NATO program. He states that I had admitted that we had done nothing in the field of economic aid. I have never made any such admission, because it would be an untrue statement if I made it. In short, Mr. Speaker, I am afraid he was tempted to make the usual C.C.F. claim to be the sole custodians of the national conscience in the cause of international economic assistance.
The background of article 2 is well known. It has been called, because of our efforts to get it in the treaty, the Canadian article. We got it included in the treaty, but only after some difficulty. Our purpose in trying to get this article in the North Atlantic treaty was a simple one, and I think one which will commend itself to the house. It was to demonstrate by the very words of our treaty that what we were signing was more than a mere military alliance; but we never at that time expected, nor do we now expect, immediate or sensational results. We were, however, anxious then, and we are anxious now, that European steps towards unity, towards greater collective action in Europe, should be tied in to the Atlantic concept, and that in their development there should be no discrimination against the overseas North Atlantic powers. We were thinking of the developments of the Brussels organization, the development of the O.E.E.C., and the arrangements for developing European agriculture and European commerce, and we were anxious that in the North Atlantic treaty there should be an article which would do what it could to ensure that these developments were on the North Atlantic and not on the European basis. Surely, that is an objective which will commend itself to all hon. members. In March, 1949, in explaining the article to the house I said this, as reported at page 2097 of Hansard, and no exception was taken to my words then:
... all we are trying to do In those words is to take a pledge that we will do our best to remove economic conflict in our international economic policy. It is a pledge, if you like, for co-operation in economic policies to the greatest extent possible and subject, of course, to our complete control over
Supply-External Affairs our own economic policies. It is hoped that by this co-operation we will help create, not only in the North Atlantic community but throughout the world, a progressive and prosperous society in which peace and security can flourish.
Mr. Speaker, I suggest that notwithstanding what has been said by the hon. members of the C.C.F. group, we are doing this in the North Atlantic Treaty Organization under article 2, and that we are building up those habits of co-operation and consultation which are referred to in that article. I believe that Canada, far from being condemned for doing nothing under the article, has done as much as or more than any other particular country to achieve its implementation by developing economic and political co-operation, and by building up the Atlantic community; but I would remind hon. members that no one country can achieve implementation of a NATO policy and that what must be done must be done by common agreement. If we look at article 2 I think we will find that, unlike certain other articles in the treaty, it does not provide specifically for any special NATO machinery; nor does it necessarily entail joint programs of action among member nations, although that might of course develop. It is a rule of conduct which member nations undertake to follow in their internal and external policies generally, and not merely in their policies vis-a-vis one another. Existing international institutions, particularly the United Nations, should be used by members to the full for this purpose. It may be that as time goes on we shall find it desirable to establish special NATO machinery and to organize special NATO programs for these broad purposes, but there is certainly no point at the present time in duplicating machinery which is already existing and which is functioning.
Meanwhile, we in NATO agree to seek under this article to eliminate conflict in our international economic policies, not only among ourselves, but as against other nations. We agree to encourage economic collaboration. I do not mean to suggest that this economic co-operation sentence of article 2 is meaningless in the sense that it is merely a guidepost for purely academic matters. It is important for other reasons. It is important as a defence against discriminatory trade practices by one NATO nation against others. It is also an extremely important safeguard should any member of NATO find its economy imperilled by reason of its contribution to the common defence of the North Atlantic community; and in setting up the T.C.C. committee to look into that very matter we were implementing article 2 of the treaty. I would also add that there is already a good deal of economic consultation and collaboration going

Supply-External Affairs on within NATO. Some of it is closely related, as is inevitable, to defence, and some less closely. Through the work, for instance, of NATO's financial and economic board I think we know more about each other's economic positions and problems than we ever knew before, and the whole of the T.C.C. operation was based on the foundation of statistics and knowledge that have been collected by the financial and economic board.
Then also, there is the defence production board which has done useful work in coordinating defence production. The usefulness of that kind of work will, I suggest, outlive- I hope it will outlive-the present emergency.
The article is being implemented in other ways, some of which do not involve the use of NATO machinery at all. As hon. members know, there are many international organizations and agencies in the economic field, and all NATO countries are members of most of them, if not all of them. It would be senseless for NATO to try to duplicate useful work being done elsewhere, and so NATO countries work through these other organizations in their efforts to further economic collaboration and avoid economic conflict.
For example, not long ago in NATO we considered setting up a special migration and manpower body, and the proposal was referred to a special committee for examination and report. But it was found, after such examination, that that was a subject much broader than NATO, that it could best be dealt with on a basis wider than NATO, and that an international organization indeed was already in existence to deal with it. Similarly, we considered setting up special NATO machinery for allocating raw materials. But it became quite clear that broader machinery, such as is now provided by the international materials conference in Washington, would meet the needs in that field much more effectively than anything NATO could do. All these matters were very carefully and very exhaustively reviewed by a special committee, and that committee did report and did recommend some concrete proposals which, I admit, have not yet been carried into action. That committee, when it gave up its mandate at Lisbon, emphasized, as indeed it had emphasized previously, that what we have done under this article is just a beginning.
We are not so concerned in NATO with talking about some grandiose or airy Atlantic NATO structure, or of setting up some rival Colombo or Marshall plan organization, as we are in laying foundations on which to build the future. But the hon. member who moved this motion will expect me to deal with the specific aspect of the charge which

he levelled at us. The charge, which was repeated this afternoon by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), was our alleged failure to provide direct economic aid to our NATO allies, which he seems to think the main or the whole purpose of article 2. It is the only part of article 2 that he talked about. He referred in this connection to the Marshall plan and emphasized that while the United States had been dealing so generously with its allies, we in Canada had provided little or nothing-a comparison against his own country which has already been noted in some United States papers. I think hon. members already know how inaccurate that kind of statement is. I believe, on the contrary, that Canada has done its full and proper share in rebuilding, consolidating and assisting the post-war free world.
The hon. member for Melfort (Mr. Wright) asks, "What has Canada done to establish economic stability in Europe to date?"-and then he answers his own question, that she "has made no real sacrifice to obtain greater security by paying some of the premium of insurance."
I would like to read out a list of the total amounts Canada has provided in various forms of economic aid since the war-that is, from the fiscal year 1945-46 up to and including the fiscal year 1951-52. Post-war financial and economic assistance during those years, in the form of credits-and that is economic assistance to Europe-amounts to $1,753 million. In the form of post-war military relief, it amounts to $95 million. By way of contributions to United Nations relief and rehabilitation agencies and assistance programs it amounts to $203 million. In connection with the Colombo plan the figure is $25,300,000; and for NATO, up to the present time, by way of mutual aid and other contributions, the figure is $324,800,000. Then there was an emergency gift of wheat to Greece of $830,000. This makes a total, of all aid given by the people of this country to those who needed it, of $2,403 million.
In the light of this well-known record I am astounded by a great many things said by the hon. member for Melfort and the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Stewart). However, the only particular point to which I wish to make special reference is the government's position on NATO mutual aid. The hon. member for Peel (Mr. Graydon) at page 678 of Hansard asked questions on that subject. He wanted to know what we had been asked to contribute to the North Atlantic peace pool, what we had undertaken to contribute, and how we would do it. He implored us to tell all.

I would be very glad indeed to tell all, so far as I know it all; but, with your permission, Mr. Speaker, I would ask that it be called five o'clock, because I understand that the sitting is to be suspended at this time.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: QUESTION AS TO COMBAT PAY FOR SOLDIERS IN KOREA
speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I should like to discuss this request for economic aid, about which we have heard so much. As has already been reported, the executive bureau of the T.C.C., known as the three wise men, approved of the general shape and size of our military program in their first report. They did, however, suggest for consideration by the Canadian government that
Supply-External Affairs in 1952-53, the current financial year, we should provide mutual aid-not of $500 million as the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) said over the air last night-but of $250 million over and above our proposed program of approximately $225 million which we had already submitted to them. That would have meant a total of $475 million for Canada for this year's NATO mutual aid. If we add in the contribution under the Colombo plan and other items it would have meant for us total foreign aid of well over $500 million.
Mr. Speaker, the government considered these proposals of the three wise men and decided that in present circumstances the amount was too high; too high in relation to our balance of payments, which is already supported by borrowing abroad at a rate in excess of $600 million a year, and indeed too high in relation to the United States itself. Indeed those figures might have meant that Canada would have been budgeting for foreign aid in larger proportion than other great nations such as the United States, and this despite the far greater per capita wealth and the stronger trading position of the United States, and despite its responsibility as a creditor nation and as the leader of our coalition. The government, however, did decide before Lisbon that it could go beyond our original program for mutual aid as submitted to the wise men. As a result, after a good deal of consideration, we decided to recommend a mutual aid program for 1952-53 of some $325 million, a figure which has already been announced and which, as it happened, is almost exactly the same figure as we have up to the present spent on mutual aid for NATO. Therefore, the total amount for foreign aid in the estimates, including the Colombo plan and other items, amounts to some $360 million for the current fiscal year. Considering all the circumstances, Mr. Speaker, I believe that this compares favourably with what any other country is likely to do.
Having decided on a total of $325 million for our NATO mutual aid, the government then had to consider how that money could best be used. Here again there was a suggestion from the three wise men that, while part of it might be spent on military equipment-they never suggested at any time that all of it should be spent on raw materials and that sort of thing-part also should be spent on raw materials, foodstuffs and so on-but not all of the $500 million as was suggested by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) last evening. This suggestion was also carefully considered by the government, and as a result we put forward an

Supply-External Affairs alternative plan which we considered to be a better one. In our reply to the TCC on January 13, we stated our position substantially as follows:
The TCC had suggested that this increased assistance might take the form partly of economic assistance and partly of military transfers. Economic aid of the type suggested would have meant forgoing payment to us for normal exports which are the basis of Canada's outgoing overseas trade. The proceeds from these exports are required to pay for our expanding import requirements, and to finance currently heavy carrying charges on external liabilities, a large part of which have been incurred in expanding the production of those same exports. We suggested to the TCC, therefore, that to give away these staple exports would cut at the basis of the viability of the Canadian economy. So we informed the TCC that, for this and for other reasons, under the present circumstances, we considered that it would be inadvisable for us to give our economic assistance in this form but that we should give it in the form of defence support. We were particularly concerned lest we should be asked to give aid in the form of raw materials because we realized that, in addition to large external payments, we would be undertaking large purchases of military equipment in the United States and large expenditures for the maintenance of our troops in the form of offshore military purchases, payment for infrastructure and other payments to NATO. We pointed out, therefore, that our mutual aid this year might better take the form of defence aid and not of the raw materials which are the basis of our export trade.
We pointed out also that, unlike the United States, Canada lived by these staple exports, that the North Atlantic treaty was a 20-year obligation, and that something like the TCC operation was clearly going to be an annual affair. As a matter of fact, later on at Lisbon we decided that that kind of examination should be an annual affair. If we started to give away our staple exports, it might very well lead us into very deep water indeed, especially at a time when we were so heavily dependent upon the United States for borrowing. We concluded, therefore, that economic aid of that type from Canada was not the best way in which we could help our NATO allies, and retain our own strength at this time. Nevertheless, the kind of help we recommended, and expect to give, is just as much economic aid as if it were in the form of raw materials. That was pointed out very clearly in this debate, I thought, by the hon. member for Grey North (Mr. Bennett). Mr. Harriman himself told congress the other

day that defence support is also a form of economic assistance, and the TCC itself has accepted that position. I hope that this explanation will answer the question on this point raised by the hon. member for Melfort (Mr. Wright) and the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Gray don).
The hon. member for Peel also addressed some questions to me on the general results of the NATO Lisbon meeting. He complained that, in spite of all I tried to say the other day, he did not yet understand what had happened. He indicated he could not understand our diplomatic language; that he was a simple, country boy and that big fancy words mean nothing to him-except, of course, when he uses them himself, which he often does with very great effect. He suggested that everything was confusion in respect of the results of the Lisbon NATO meeting, and the cause of this confusion- others on the opposite side of the house have affirmed this-was that press release which I suspect, Mr. Speaker, is the only document emanating from the Lisbon meeting that a good many members, who have criticized it, have yet read.

speechtext:
It did indeed. In respect of this press release, the hon. member for Peel said that I was the culprit, and the leader of the opposition demanded an explanation of the circumstances under which it became public.	Why, he said, was this phantom
army paraded to irritate the Russians who knew perfectly well it was not accurate? Indeed, the member for Rosetown-Biggar, going I thought a little bit far in a radio broadcast last night, subscribed to the characterization of this press release as a downright lie. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that it was not, and could not fairly be so characterized.
This now famous press release was, of course, not any statement from the Secretary of State for External Affairs, nor was it a Canadian statement. It was not even a council communique. It was a press communique on a statement of the TCC which had been adopted by the council. Indeed, it was not even correctly quoted in the house the other evening by the leader of the opposition. There was no mention in that press release, or in any other release from the Lisbon meeting, of a figure of 100 divisions as the leader of the opposition indicated the other night when he claimed at page 870 of Hansard, that the statement said:
. . . that we would have fifty divisions toward the end of 1952, and that a hundred divisions were expected by 1954 . . .

Indeed the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar also suggested that the statement indicated that we would have 100 divisions by the end of 1954. The statement made no reference to any figure of any kind except approximately 50 divisions in appropriate stages of combat readiness by the end of 1952. I do not know the source of this figure of 100 divisions which has been attributed to this press release. The inaccuracy of such a statement could easily have been confirmed by reading the press release.
I was the chairman of the Lisbon council meeting, Mr. Speaker, and of course the chairman must accept the responsibility, as chairman, for everything that is issued in the name of the council. It is fair that he should do so. But in view of the statements that have been made about this press release, I think it might be of some interest to the house-and I would not mention this matter if so much attention had not been directed to the press release-if I indicated how this statement became public.
The wording of the paragraph in the statement which has caused so much controversy and which has been repeated so many times, in the form in which it appeared, was supplied to the council by the members of the T.C.C. who drafted the statement-members representing the United Kingdom, the United States and France: Sir Edwin Plowden, Mr. Harriman and Mr. Monnet. After drafting by the T.C.C., it was approved by the ministers of defence of these nations, or at least by a United Kingdom cabinet minister, Lord Ismay, acting for the minister of defence, and by a senior representative of France. It was also approved in the form in which it appeared by the chairman of the NATO standing group, General Bradley. It was also approved by General Eisenhower's deputy, General Gruen-ther. After that consideration and approval it was sent to the chairman for clearance.
